A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Process Reward Agents work. The complete text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, cross-policy transfer results, ablations and retrieval analyses in Tables 1–4 and Figures 2–5.

after.justification: v2 retains these original empirical studies and reports revised PRA accuracies in Tables 1–4.

M1.justification: The reward agent, retrieval controller, label construction, reward readout and beam-search procedure are retained. Adding q explicitly to the controller and reward equations clarifies an input already present in v1's prompts; the appendix formatting revisions do not establish a new algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions train on MedQA and evaluate MedQA, Medbullets, MedMCQA, MMLU-Med, GPQA, Lancet and NEJM using the same medical knowledge corpora. More training traces per question change sample quantity, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain Direct, CoT and RAG with and without self-consistency, the same cross-policy comparators, untrained reward agents, and post hoc PRA aggregation variants. The newly cited medical-RAG works are not added as evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes training-data generation from one to eight reasoning traces for each of 10,178 MedQA questions, substantially increasing the reported training-sample budget. Appendix D also revises prompt formats. Evaluation coverage, retrieval settings, beam width, branching factor and self-consistency budgets remain unchanged. These are reported setting revisions, not proof that every experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: The training/search and reward-timing ablations in Tables 3–4 revise the full online PRA result from 80.8 to 81.9, changing the reported gaps to retained controls. Their tested factors and other result entries are unchanged. The scaling, selective-search and margin-shift analyses retain their existing plots and questions.

E5.justification: Figure 2 retains 1,000 Monte Carlo trials for self-consistency and bootstrap uncertainty over questions, displayed as ±1 standard error. The other uncertainty displays are retained, with no new seed or repeated-run reporting. The increased training-trace count is not an increase in independent experimental repetitions.

E6.justification: Central PRA results are substantially revised under the changed reported training setup. Table 1 replaces MedQA 80.8 with 81.9, Medbullets 63.6 with 65.9, Lancet 67.0 with 70.9, and the average 71.0 with 72.1; NEJM changes from 68.3 to 68.0. Table 2 revises five policies' PRA scores, including Qwen2.5-3B from 69.9 to 74.9, and Llama-3.1-8B overtakes Qwen3-4B. Baseline scores remain unchanged; these are not established same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The assumptions, objective, cumulative-reward definition and margin-shift equations retain their mathematical substance. Explicit question arguments and the added retriever entry in Table 5 clarify existing notation. Neither version adds theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction update the headline MedQA accuracy claim from 80.8% to 81.9%. The three stated contributions, claimed state of the art at the 4B scale, transfer across 0.5B–8B policies and maximum 25.7-point improvement retain their scope.

C2.justification: Explanations concerning online reward guidance, latent policy capabilities, selective retrieval and margin-shift patterns are retained. The Impact Statement preserves the qualifications that hallucinations can remain and the system is not ready for clinical deployment.

D1.justification: Appendix D revises reproducibility instructions: the policy prompt adds an Answer suffix and changes option formatting; the teacher requests a tagged [REASONING_SCORE] output; the PRA template distinguishes prior steps from the current candidate and clarifies document insertion. Appendix C's optimizer settings, epochs and precision, and the code/data access information, remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2.1 adds Sohn et al. (2025), Rationale-guided retrieval augmented generation for medical question answering, and Kim et al. (2025a), Rethinking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine. These modestly broaden the medical-RAG references without changing the central positioning against post hoc reward models.

P1.justification: v2 corrects grammar and typographical errors, removes a duplicated scoring explanation, fixes the pseudocode reference from Figure B to Figure 6, standardizes terminology and expands prompt captions. The main narrative and section order remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: The document adopts an ICML proceedings layout, changing typography, column geometry, headings, running headers, captions and float placement throughout. Figure 1 revises node styling and evidence-flow arrows, and appendix prompt boxes are reformatted. All nine figures and five tables are retained; the empirical plots are redisplayed rather than newly added.

improvement.justification: v2 modestly improves clarity through explicit question conditioning, corrected cross-references, more detailed prompt specifications and two relevant medical-RAG citations. Higher reported scores accompany an eightfold training-trace budget and do not alone establish better paper quality. The documentation gains are limited by a new ambiguity: Figure 8 requests a tagged teacher output while Section 4.1 still describes emitting a single token.
